name: Beta-sitosterol / plant sterols
short: Sitosterolaemia (rare, genetic): sterols build up; xanthomas, early artery disease (review: LDL seems the main cause). Gene studies link high plant sterols to heart disease; long-term safety unknown.
text: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, a systematic review of 4 double-blind placebo-controlled trials of beta-sitosterol (519 men, 4 to 26 weeks) found similar withdrawal rates with beta-sitosterol and placebo (7.8% vs 8.0%), but the abstract does not list adverse effects, and the reviewers said long-term effectiveness and safety are unknown. Sitosterolaemia is a rare inherited disorder (ABCG5 or ABCG8 gene mutations) in which plasma plant sterol levels are extremely elevated, characterised by tendon and tuberous xanthomas, premature vascular disease and arthritis (case report and reviews); one review of the disorder says that accumulated evidence, including infant cases, has shown that raised LDL cholesterol, and not raised sitosterol, seems to be the major cause of its atherosclerosis. In a small randomized crossover trial, 10 people carrying one copy of an ABCG8 mutation and 15 controls took about 1.6 g of plant sterol capsules daily for 4 weeks; LDL cholesterol fell in both groups and blood plant sterol concentrations rose in both groups (carriers 39.72 μmol/L with plant sterols vs 27.32 with placebo; controls 24.03 vs 21.12; the abstract reports no test of the difference between the two groups), and the authors suggest that carrying the mutation does not influence the effect of plant sterols on blood cholesterol but may affect sterol absorption. For plant sterols and stanols more broadly (mostly in enriched foods), reviews describe the following cautions: an expert review found that sterol-enriched foods raise plasma plant sterol levels and lower beta-carotene levels (although it did not expect adverse health outcomes from the beta-carotene fall), called the resulting cardiovascular risk largely hypothetical, found vitamin A and D levels unaffected, and found insufficient data to say whether plant stanols or sterols prevent or promote colon cancer; a 2023 review notes the lack of randomized trials of long-term safety and that genetic studies link elevated circulating plant sterols with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, raising safety concerns; and a 2015 review argues that plant sterol supplementation may even be harmful. For interactions, one review describes controversy over whether statins further raise plasma non-cholesterol sterols, raising concerns about the safety of adding plant sterols to those drugs.
